title: Optical centrifuge as a probe of strong dissipative coupling between a molecular rotor and superfluid helium
authors: Ian MacPhail-Bartley, Sören E. Mahr, Cameron E. Peters, Baptiste Coquinot, Volker Karle, Giacomo Bighin, Ragheed Alhyder, Mikhail Lemeshko, Henrik Stapelfeldt, Valery Milner
abstract: A macroscopic manifestation of superfluidity is that objects moving through liquid helium experience negligible friction below the Landau critical velocity. How this frictionless motion breaks down at the nanoscale remains an open question. Molecules embedded in helium nanodroplets represent a well-controlled system for studying this breakdown, yet none has reached the regime of strong dissipative coupling, when energy transfer from the molecule to the superfluid dominates the observed dynamics. Molecular rotation, induced by short laser pulses, offer a suitable probe to reach rotational energies in the range of the roton gap, where superfluid helium supports a large number of elementary excitations. However, the solvation shell around a rotating molecule caps the energy reachable by a free rotor after impulsive excitation well below the roton excitation energy. Here we show that continuous driving with an ultraslow optical centrifuge overcomes this limitation: the strong field dresses the molecule into pendular states whose energies fall within the spectrum of the collective excitations of the superfluid, placing the system in the strong-dissipation regime. The resulting rapid thermalization locks the molecule to the rotating field until the rotation-induced level splittings overtake the thermalization rate, beyond which the molecular alignment is progressively lost. Our approach offers a direct measurement of the molecule-bath coupling in a quantum fluid.
summary: This paper investigates molecular rotation in superfluid helium using an optical centrifuge to probe strong dissipative coupling. By continuously driving the rotor, the system is forced into a regime where molecular energy matches the superfluid excitation spectrum. The resulting dynamics allow researchers to directly measure the molecule-bath coupling strength by tracking the decay of molecular alignment.
main_problem: The research aims to understand the breakdown of frictionless motion at the nanoscale when objects move through superfluid helium, specifically reaching the regime of strong dissipative coupling.
main_result: The use of an ultraslow optical centrifuge successfully drives the system into the strong-dissipation regime, allowing for a direct measurement of the molecule-bath coupling strength by observing the loss of molecular alignment.
method: The study combines experimental techniques (VMI, optical centrifuging) with theoretical modeling using master equations and time-dependent Lindblad dynamics to simulate the rotor-bath interaction.
model_or_system: The system involves molecular rotors ($	ext{CS}_2$, $	ext{OCS}$) embedded in superfluid helium, driven by a time-varying optical centrifuge field. The dynamics are modeled using a Hamiltonian in the rotating frame coupled to a thermal bath via a master equation.
key_observables: The degree of molecular alignment, $\langle \cos^2 	heta_{2D} angle(t)$, is the primary diagnostic observable, tracked via time-resolved measurements and spectrograms.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the Landau critical velocity, the centrifugal wall limit, and the characteristic thermalization rate ($	au$) which defines the strong-dissipation regime.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on phenomenological master equations and Lindblad ansatzes to model the bath interaction, and the steady-state construction is noted to omit transient memory effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the VMI geometry and time evolution of the alignment signal $\langle \cos^2 	heta_{2D} angle(t)$ for $	ext{CS}_2$ in both jets and droplets, comparing model predictions (Lindblad vs. steady-state) against experimental data.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical problem (dissipation in superfluid helium), introducing the optical centrifuge as a novel probe, developing the theoretical framework (Hamiltonian and master equation), and finally comparing model predictions (steady-state vs. time-dependent Lindblad) against experimental measurements for both $	ext{CS}_2$ and $	ext{OCS}$.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it tackles open quantum systems problems—specifically, how coherent quantum dynamics are modified and controlled by strong coupling to a complex quantum bath (superfluid helium).

figures.caption: Figure 1. Geometry of the Velocity Map Imaging experiment. The magenta corkscrew represents the electric field of the optical centrifuge (⃗ECFG), propagating to the right along the y axis. The VMI spectrometer, oriented along the z axis, projects the ion fragment velocities onto the xy plane of the detector. θ2D is the angle of a detected ion fragment, measured with respect to the xz plane of centrifuge rotation. A carbon disulfide (CS2) molecule inside a helium droplet is shown aligned to the centrifuge, with a simulated distribution of S+ fragments shown below. The inset illustrates ⟨cos2 θ2D⟩(t) for a molecule following the rotation of ⃗ECFG during the initial portion of the centrifuge...

Figure 2. Degree of alignment in the ensemble of centrifuged CS2 molecules, expressed as ⟨cos2 θ2D⟩(t) (blue markers with red error bars) and measured in (a) the seeded molecular jet, and (c) helium nanodroplets. Blue lines connect the data points to help guide the eye. Applying a short-time Fourier transform to both signals results in the corresponding two-dimensional spectrograms, shown in panels (b) and (d). The white dashed line in panel (d) marks the “centrifugal wall” of the CS2-helium complex, occurring around 22 GHz (Ref. 18).

Figure 3. The alignment dynamics of CS2 molecules embedded in helium droplets spun by accelerating and decelerating ultraslow optical centrifuges, with ⟨cos2 θ2D⟩(t) shown in (a) and (b), respectively. The experimental data (connected blue diamonds) is compared with the results of our numerical simulations (red traces).

Figure 4. (a) The alignment dynamics of centrifuged OCS molecules embedded in helium droplets. The experimental data (connected blue diamonds) is compared with the results of our numerical simulations (red traces). (b) Short-time Fourier transform, with the “centrifugal wall’ indicated by the white dashed line.

Figure 5. ⟨cos2 θ2D⟩signal averaged over the random initial orientation of the centrifuge polarization (see Supplementary Information for details). Connected blue (magenta) diamonds with red error bars correspond to CS2 (OCS) molecules embedded in helium droplets.
